newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IFC urges Pakistan to start hedge trade in cotton.
newsitem.headline: IFC urges Pakistan to start hedge trade in cotton.

text.p: The International Finance Corporation (IFC), the World Bank's private lending arm, said on Monday it was trying to convince Pakistan to start hedge trading in cotton to help its agriculture and textile sectors.

"Forward trading is good for agriculture and for the textile sector, which are both linked to cotton," Andre Hovaguimian, IFC director for Central Asia, Middle East and North Africa, told a news conference.
The government lifted a 21-year ban on forward trade in cotton in May 1995 but the decision has not been implemented due to resistance from ginners who cite religious objections.
The private Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association opposes forward trading on the grounds that any transaction without delivery of goods is not allowed in Islamic Sharia (law).
Hovaguimian questioned whether hedging was really against Islamic precepts. "Future trading is not gambling...the forward market permits you to lock in a price in the future," he said.
He said Pakistani textile manufacturers had to keep large stocks of cotton in the absence of forward cover, causing liquidity problems. "That affects prices and quality," he said.
Hovaguimian said the IFC was discussing the hedging issue with government officials and was ready to assist in setting up a commodity exchange in Pakistan.

The IFC had invested $404 million in Pakistan in 1995/96 (July-June) in financial, infrastructure, manufacturing and education projects, against $352 million in 1994/95. "This year we had a record investment in Pakistan," he added.
